title: Lambdas, closures and captured variables
body: A lambda can use variables from its enclosing scope; the lambda plus those variables is a closure. C# captures variables, not values: the compiler moves captured locals into a hidden class instance shared by the method and the lambda. A later change to the variable is visible to the lambda, and the lambda can change it too.

`foreach` gives each iteration a fresh loop variable, so lambdas created in a `foreach` capture different variables. A `for` loop has one counter variable for the whole loop: every lambda captures the same `i` and sees its final value. Copy it into a local inside the body (`int copy = i;`) to capture per-iteration values.

Capturing allocates the closure object and keeps captured variables (and anything they reference) alive as long as the delegate lives. A `static` lambda (`static x => x * 2`) cannot capture, which the compiler enforces (CS8820); use it on hot paths to guarantee no hidden allocation and pass state explicitly instead.

Lambdas can declare parameter types, attributes and a return type (`int (string s) => s.Length`), use discards (`(_, _) => 0`), and have default parameter values (C# 12). C# 14 allows modifiers like `out`, `ref`, `in` and `scoped` on implicitly typed lambda parameters: `TryParse<int> p = (text, out result) => int.TryParse(text, out result);`.
Check what each lambda captures, whether it captures a shared loop counter, and whether storing the delegate extends the lifetime of large objects.
challenge: Write MakeAccumulator(int start) returning a Func<int,int> that adds its argument to a running total captured in a closure. Show that two accumulators keep independent totals.
question: Three lambdas created in `for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)` each return i. What do they return when called after the loop?
wrong: A compile error because i is out of scope
reasoning: A for loop has one i shared by every closure; foreach creates a fresh variable per iteration.
